definition: Escalate means to rise, or make something rise, level by level — a conflict, demand, or cost climbing by stages, each more serious than the last.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word escalate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know escalate should be able to work it out from your sentence.

The scandal never spread beyond a single echelon of the ministry — those above it never learned, and those below never guessed.
Escalate means to rise, or make something rise, level by level — a conflict, demand, or cost climbing by stages, each more serious than the last.

What began as a quarrel over a hedge escalated by degrees: clipped remarks in the driveway, then surveyor's stakes, then a letter from a lawyer, until two households that had traded casseroles for a decade stopped waving.
Escalate is the ladder verb: trouble that escalates does not merely grow, it moves up rungs — remark to stake to lawyer — and every rung climbed is harder to climb back down.
That stepwise rise, level by named level, is what separates escalating from simply getting worse.
neutral — news, business, and diplomatic writing
Escalate frames a rise as a climb up identifiable levels, which is why it dominates reporting on conflicts, disputes, and prices: each step can be named, and each is harder to reverse.

When something merely grows stronger with no rungs to point to, intensify is the more accurate verb; and when you raise a problem to a higher authority on purpose — 'escalate the ticket' — the word is doing its ladder work in an office instead of a war room.

The cafeteria's 'condiment war' started as a joke.
In week one, someone hid the ketchup.
In week two, the lunch crew retaliated by labeling every sauce in Latin.
Then the pranks escalated: a mustard fountain appeared in the teachers' lounge, and the principal's parking space was outlined in relish packets.
Each round was a level graver than the last, and by October the school board had scheduled a hearing — a stage nobody had believed a joke could reach.
Veteran teachers knew the shape at once: nothing about the war grew louder or larger so much as it climbed, rung by rung, toward real consequences.
